project_lysandra_context_1: Lysandra is a tactical open-world action RPG made by Faill Studio. The player is Lyra, travelling through the world of Era.
project_lysandra_context_2: The demo is playable: it is downloaded with the Faill launcher.
project_lysandra_role: Lead programmer in a team of 7. Lilian is also the only developer of everything around the game: the site, the Faill launcher and the API that distributes the updates.
project_lysandra_built_1: The Faill launcher, in Tauri 2, with signed updates.
project_lysandra_built_2: The distribution API, which serves the launcher its update files on two channels: release and preview.
project_lysandra_built_3: The game's site, whose media are stored on Cloudflare R2.
project_lysandra_built_4: The game's architecture and the player's state machine.
project_lysandra_built_5: Combat: Gameplay Ability System, targeting and poise.
project_lysandra_built_6: The monsters' AI, with a hierarchical state machine and Utility AI.
project_lysandra_built_7: The camera with Cinemachine, saving, quests and cutscenes.
project_lysandra_built_8: The bosses and the visual effects, shared with another programmer.
project_lysandra_built_9: Automated tests, and 16 recorded architecture decisions.
project_huzounet_context_1: Huzounet is Huz Studio's site, the reference for Dofus's online mode. Lilian is its developer.
project_huzounet_context_2: It brings together equipment (PvM and PvP builds), monsters and bosses, the market (prices per server and crafting returns), guides and tools: Dofmaster, Carte du monde, Familier, Brisage and PNJ Dofus. The Huz browser extension completes the site.
project_huzounet_context_3: More than 500,000 unique visitors use it every month (Cloudflare figure, November 2026).
project_huzounet_role: Sole developer of the site and all its tools. A rewrite of the site in TanStack Start is in beta.
project_huzounet_built_1: The site, in Next.js with Payload CMS and PostgreSQL.
project_huzounet_built_2: The community market, which reads players' screenshots with OCR, right in the browser.
project_huzounet_built_4: The PNJ Dofus desktop app, in Tauri 2.
project_huzounet_built_5: The Huz extension for Chrome, Firefox and Edge.
project_huzounet_built_6: The extractor of the Dofus 3 client data, and the API that serves it.
project_atelier_context_1: Atelier is an open-source visual scripting core for Unity. A gameplay behaviour has three parts: a trigger, conditions, then instructions run in order.
project_atelier_context_2: You assemble it in the Inspector or write it with the C# API, and both drive the same core. Designers assemble, programmers extend.
project_atelier_context_3: The Core package is at version 0.1.0: its API may still change before 1.0.
project_atelier_role: Alone on the project: design and development of the core, its editors and its identity.

project_atelier_built_2: The Inspector editors, including an instruction picker sorted by category.
project_atelier_built_3: The C# API, which lets programmers extend Atelier, for example with a new condition.
project_atelier_built_4: Atelier's identity: logo, banner and icons.

agents_meta_title: Working with AI agents, Lilian PRIEU's method
agents_meta_description: How Lilian PRIEU works with coding agents: a public method, tests first, an independent review, and this portfolio as a case study.
agents_lede: Coding agents write fast and get things wrong with confidence. This is the method I built so they understand before they code, prove what they deliver and leave the decisions to me.
agents_short_read: Short on time? The sections marked “Essential” are enough to get the idea. The others go into detail, for engineers.
agents_why_1: A coding agent reads a request, writes code and announces that it is done. For a small change, that is enough. On a real project, I saw the same mistakes come back: it builds before it understands, asks me what the repository already says, judges its own work and publishes without asking.
agents_why_quote: Agents fail in predictable ways: they build before understanding the request, ask you what the repository already says, grade their own work, bury you in jargon or in ceremony, and publish without asking. The stack answers each failure with an opinion.
agents_why_2: None of these mistakes comes from a lack of coding skill. They come from how the work is organized. The method answers them with written rules, stored as skills: instruction files an agent loads when a task needs them. One rule per observed mistake.
agents_origins_1: Before writing rules, I wrote tools. I wanted to use Claude's and ChatGPT's models in the Cursor editor, with the subscriptions I already had. So I wrote three proxies in turn: small servers that pass Cursor's requests on to those services.
agents_origins_2: Then I gave agents abilities they lacked, as MCP servers (Model Context Protocol, the protocol that lets an agent call an outside program): generating pictures for a website, inspecting a running Tauri application.
agents_origins_3: These tools solved access to the models, not the quality of the work. `tauri-agent-kit` is now part of the method: agent-skills' Tauri skill asks agents to use it. The `imagegen` skill makes pictures another way, through the Codex CLI. Reading it as the successor of `gemini-image-mcp` is my interpretation: the repository states no such link.

agents_path_1: Everything starts with one command, `/work`, followed by the request in plain words. The agent reads the code, the tests and the history, then restates what will change and how we will know it works.
agents_path_2: It then sizes the request. Quick: a short fix with no open decision. Small: one unit of work, tracked in a Linear issue. Project: several units, tracked in a Linear project. The ceremony grows with the request, never beyond it.
agents_path_caption: The path of a request, after the diagram in agent-skills' README.
agents_path_quote: Only an explicit yes to the latest version is agreement; silence or a yes to an earlier version is not.
agents_path_3: Nothing is coded without that agreement. Then come the tests, the review and the demonstration. Publishing the branch, merging and deploying each wait for my yes.
agents_step_request_detail: `/work` and the request, in plain words.
agents_step_size_detail: Quick, Small or Project. A bug, a research question or an experiment goes through `debug`, `research` or `prototype` first.
agents_step_interview_detail: Small or Project: open decisions are settled through short questions (`interview`).
agents_step_agreement_detail: An explicit yes to the latest version of the plan.
agents_step_build_detail: Tests first: every behavior starts with a failing test.
agents_step_show_detail: The result runs where the user will use it.
agents_step_ship_detail: Only when the user says yes.
agents_memory_heading: Linear as memory, one unit per session
agents_memory_1: An agent forgets everything from one conversation to the next, and its attention thins out in a conversation that runs too long. So the method does not rely on its memory. What was decided, what was learned and what remains lives in Linear, an issue tracker: every Small change is an issue, every Project a project.
agents_memory_2: An issue is written for a reader who has neither the conversation nor the code in mind: current behavior, expected behavior, decisions, acceptance criteria, out of scope. Each one has a type: Task, Bug, Research, Prototype or Interview.
agents_memory_quote: It stops at its handoff and the next starts from Linear, so each starts with a fresh context and the user judges one result at a time.
agents_memory_3: So a session does one thing, then stops. Before this rule, one conversation chained several units: context piled up and I had several results to judge at once.
agents_evidence_1: Every behavior starts with a failing test, written where a caller uses the code: a page address, a command, a public function. The agent reads the failure to check that it shows the missing behavior, not a broken setup, then writes the code that makes it pass.
agents_evidence_2: A passing test is not enough. The agent runs the result the way the user will: it opens the page, runs the command, records the walkthrough. Its report starts with what I can check myself.
agents_evidence_quote: A change is done when its checks ran and the user can see the result working.
agents_review_1: An agent reviewing its own code finds its own reasoning there, and so its own blind spots. The review goes to other agents that start from a blank context. They get the change and the sources, but neither the author's reasoning nor the other reviewers' findings.
agents_review_2: They review along three axes: requirements (does the change do what was asked?), the project's standards, and correctness. Each finding is checked before it is fixed, and the fixes are reviewed in turn. When the review could not be independent, the report says so.
agents_review_quote: Agreement between agents does not establish correctness.

agents_case_2: The review found real defects. On the home page (PR #7), it caught a mislabeled Huzounet figure, links with ambiguous names and a missing space before a label: all were fixed, then reviewed again. PR #8, which only added pictures, says openly that it had no code review.
agents_case_3: Dead ends stay visible. A dark 3D room, then a passage from the real world to a virtual one, were prototyped and dropped. The site was first built with Astro, then rebuilt with TanStack Start.
agents_evolution_heading: A method that changes and is shared
agents_evolution_1: The method is public, in the agent-skills repository, and each skill installs on its own. The figures below date from November 9, 2026.
agents_evolution_stat_skills: skills, 6 of them for the path of a request
agents_evolution_2: It changes through pull requests, like code, and each one says what it did not check.
agents_evolution_changes_label: Pull requests that changed the method
agents_change_112: A first modular workflow, with tests first built into implementation.
agents_change_112_gap: single runs, which do not establish reliability.
agents_change_127: An orchestrator, `triage`, and the independent review on three axes.
agents_change_127_gap: the Linear workflows were not exercised end to end.
agents_change_170: The README rewritten around the method and its diagram.
agents_change_170_gap: neither the diagram's rendering checked nor an agent trial.
agents_change_182: `/work` replaces the former workflow and all tracking goes through Linear. Four trials with a simulated user.
agents_change_182_gap: delegated research and parallel units were never reached in the trials.
agents_evolution_3: These declared gaps are where the next piece of work starts: they say where to look next.
